 Plan Choice Counseling and Accessibility for Dual-Eligible Beneficiaries
 By 
 Jisoo Choi 
 November 19, 2026 
 No Comments 
 Loading the Elevenlabs Text to Speech AudioNative Player… 
 With Medicare’s Fall Open Enrollment period in full swing, Medicare Advantage (MA) and Part D beneficiaries across the country are reviewing their plan benefits and directories to make coverage decisions for next year. For people who are dually eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid, plan enrollment—whether during Fall Open Enrollment or another time—comes with even more considerations.
 The latest case study in our policy series, Making Medicare and Medicaid Work Better Together , recounts the experiences of two dual-eligible beneficiaries who received plan choice counseling from Medicare Rights Center counselors.
 Navigating Integrated Plan Choices
 Dual-eligible special needs plans (D-SNPs) , a type of MA Plan, can be a good option for integrated care that manages Medicare and Medicaid together. Still, the lack of beneficiary resources about them can make D-SNPs inaccessible to those who could most benefit from them. 
 The lack of beneficiary resources about them can make D-SNPs inaccessible to those who could most benefit from them. 
 Ms. W, already enrolled in Medicaid, turned 65 and became eligible for Medicare. Because her Medicaid Managed Care insurer also offered D-SNPs, she received a default enrollment notice informing her that she will automatically be switched to the insurer’s D-SNP. But the notice contained neither information specific to her providers and medications nor details about other choices that were available to her as she entered Medicare, such as other MA options or Original Medicare. When she called Medicare Rights, a counselor explained to Ms. W all her enrollment options, including D-SNPs. They asked Ms. W about her experiences with her current insurer, as well as about the providers and prescriptions she needed, and they were able to not only help Ms. W make a decision for her current needs but also empower her with information to help her navigate plans in the future.
 We were able to help Ms. W make a decision for her current needs and empower her with information to help her navigate plans in the future.
 Mr. J reached out to Medicare Rights during Open Enrollment when he learned that his D-SNP, which had met his coverage needs for six years, would be terminating. He had received advertisements from various other MA plans touting their integrated options, supplemental benefits, and extra perks, but he had no way of comparing their coverage to his current plan. His Medicare Rights counselor helped him review his coverage needs to decide what to prioritize while comparing plans. For Mr. J, these included non-emergency medical transportation, which only some MA plans offered. With a clearer idea of what he was looking for in a plan, Mr. J was able to cut through the noise of MA marketing to find the integrated plan that suited him best.
 Policy Directions
 Both Ms. W and Mr. J needed counseling and support that met them where they were. Some beneficiaries, especially those enrolling in Medicare or Medicaid for the first time, feel overwhelmed and need someone to help them understand their options. Others may be receiving a flood of information designed to influence their decision-making or hook them on extra benefits. Whatever their situation, beneficiaries need an unbiased resource to guide them through plan comparisons.
 Beneficiaries need an unbiased resource to guide them through plan comparisons.
 In addition to counseling like ours, dual-eligible beneficiaries must have better resources and support. Default enrollment notifications like Ms. W’s should have comprehensive information on Medicare and give beneficiaries the time and resources to make enrollment decisions. States should support their dual-eligible population through counseling via ombudsman programs and dedicated Medicare–Medicaid offices to handle integration issues and progress policies for dual-eligible coverage.
 Read the case study series, Making Medicare and Medicaid Work Better Together .
